transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-06-07 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Location: Zoom / Fireflies.ai transcript
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (Northleaf), Leah Kim (Northleaf), Evan Rivera (Northleaf), Priya Verma (Northleaf)

Summary: quick sync then deep lab walk-through, live Q/A, identify artifacts to share and next steps.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. This is Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Omar is our SE who'll lead the lab portion. We'll start with a quick topology recap then jump into the perf and DNS hairpin scenarios.
00:18 Samir Rao: Awesome. Goal for us is reproducing the intermittent 200–600ms tail spikes we've been seeing when traffic routes out and back in through the NAT. We think it correlates with KV miss storms but also saw broken TLS handshakes earlier.
00:32 Omar Patel: Right. Hi all — Omar here. Two threads: first the network egress path (nat vs privatelink, hairpinning), second the runtime KV/cache and batching behavior when tokens come back in.
00:50 Leah Kim: Quick security note — we need to validate KMS/HSM flows on any private path. We can't have secrets traverse public egress even temporarily.
01:02 Maya Chen: Understood. We'll include the Private VPC KMS diagram. Quick question: are you using a single NAT gateway across AZs or per-AZ?
01:12 Evan Rivera: Single NAT for cost reasons. Route tables are per-subnet but internet egress goes to that one NAT in AZ-a. We suspect it gets saturated and then hairpins back via a different path.
01:28 Omar Patel: That explains asymmetric routing. Single NAT can TTL out connections and when the response arrives from a different backend, resolver behavior and TLS session resumption may fail causing cold starts in the runtime.
01:41 Priya Verma: And that matches the KV cache misses — when TLS restarts, the connection isn't reusing the KV cache affinity, right?
01:54 Omar Patel: Exactly. A big point: our KV cache is process-local with optional inter-pod sharding. If requests are sticky to a particular GPU pod, you get very high hit rate. But with hairpin/egress-induced fanout, requests land on different pods and you see coherence problems — effectively a distributed cold-start.
02:12 Samir Rao: Could we force session affinity at the LB level? We run Envoy with a 2 min timeout.
02:20 Maya Chen: Envoy sticky cookie helps but only if your egress and route tables preserve client source. With NAT and SNAT you get different 5-tuples, and cookies don't always help if the source IP changes. PrivateLink keeps source consistent because it doesn't SNAT, so affinity holds.
02:36 Leah Kim: So PrivateLink sounds safer for stateful affinity — but we have cost controls dictating NAT for now. Any mitigations short-term?
02:45 Omar Patel: Short-term: tune TCP/TLS reuse — increase keepalive, enable session resumption (TLS tickets), and set kernel netfilter conntrack timeouts to keep mappings longer. Also runtime-wise, enable a small cross-pod memcached layer for KV cold-starts so misses don't hit model disk.
03:05 Samir Rao: When you say small memcached layer, do you mean externalizing KV cache off the GPU process? Won't that kill latency?
03:12 Omar Patel: Tradeoff: remote memcached adds ~250–500us for a hit vs 0–50us local hit. But it's orders of magnitude better than a model reload or cold KV cold path which is tens of milliseconds. So it's a win if you use it as L2, not primary.
03:31 Priya Verma: What about batching parameters? We saw p50 good but p95 terrible during spikes.
03:38 Omar Patel: Batching is the other lever. If your batch window is too long to accumulate tokens, latency spikes when you form huge batches. Conversely too small batches waste GPU cycles. We usually recommend dynamic batching with a 8–20ms target latency cap for interactive apps and a max batch size tuned to model footprint and GPU memory.
03:55 Maya Chen: Also quantization can change token processing speed — INT8 can speed per-token perf but it sometimes increases variance due to kernel selection differences on different GPUs.
04:10 Evan Rivera: We're running mixed FP16 + some quantized weights for cost reasons; we've seen odd p95 regressions post-quantization. Any guidance?
04:20 Omar Patel: Important to test model fidelity and runtime stability. Some kernels fall back to slower paths on edge cases with INT8. For Private deployments, we recommend doing an A/B on a dedicated pool with identical batch patterns and sequence lengths to validate p95. Also pre-warm KV caches and run a synthetic traffic replayer matching your real user sequences — especially the prefix distributions.
04:46 Samir Rao: Let's talk DNS specifics — we saw resolver NXTTL spikes and long lookup times causing overall request stalls.
04:53 Omar Patel: Hairpin/DNS interplay: when egress goes out and back in, the resolver may see the same internal host as external and return external IPs, causing hairpin NAT issues. Also if you have conditional forwarders, cache misses can cascade. We want to see your resolver config — are you using local resolver per-subnet or a centralized one?
05:13 Evan Rivera: Centralized resolver (managed). We do conditional forwarding for internal domains to the on-prem resolver that then forwards out, so there's a chain.
05:22 Omar Patel: Chains increase tail. For labs we replicate a two-hop resolver chain and insert TTL and packet loss to reproduce. Tools: dig with +tries and tc qdisc netem for latency.
05:39 Maya Chen: Can you quickly share the artifacts we'll need? Evan?
05:42 Evan Rivera: Yes — route tables, nat instance id, resolver config, and some perf traces. I'll upload them after.
05:49 Maya Chen: Great. Now I'll hand to Omar for the lab sketch and proposed perf harness.
05:53 Omar Patel: Lab plan high level: 1) replay recorded traffic into a Redwood private deployment in your VPC with single NAT configured, measure p50/p95 and KV miss ratio; 2) flip to per-AZ NAT or PrivateLink emulation and re-run; 3) enable L2 memcached and TLS session tweaks and measure delta; 4) run quantized model on a mirrored pool and compare latency distributions. We'll instrument (stacks: eBPF tcp/conntrack, envoy stats, runtime token timers).
06:30 Samir Rao: Sounds good. How long to prep the harness?
06:33 Omar Patel: We can prep an initial harness in about 3 business days; full lab reproducible run takes a week including data transfer and logs.
06:44 Leah Kim: On compliance — we need to confirm session ticket encryption uses our KMS key and that PrivateLink paths avoid public egress.
06:53 Maya Chen: We'll include KMS usage notes; PrivateLink keeps control plane inside the VPC and avoids SNAT so good for compliance. We'll also share the SAML and audit log retention docs.
07:03 Priya Verma: Anything else for the topology? MTU and SNI? We had one incident suspected to be MTU fragmentation.
07:12 Omar Patel: MTU matters for KV cache transfers and model shard fetches. If MTU is mismatched you can see PMTU blackholes and TCP retransmits causing significant latency. For SNI and TLS SNI mismatch, ensure egress proxies pass SNI intact. Also enable TCP Fast Open where possible to shave a RTT.
07:38 Evan Rivera: We do see retransmits, will check PMTU.
07:42 Maya Chen: A couple of quick notes on quantization: QAT (quantized-aware training) tends to keep p95 stable versus post-training static quant; also group-wise per-channel quant tends to preserve fidelity. We'll send a short note with recommended quant configs used in Redwood's benchmarks.
08:02 Omar Patel: For batching knobs: prefer adaptive batch flush that prioritizes latency SLOs. Example: flush if wait > 12 ms or batchSize >= 64 or token budget reached. Also consider model-splitting for very long sequences to avoid huge KV growth.
08:21 Samir Rao: Model-splitting — you mean segment longer prompts? We have chat contexts that reach 4k tokens.
08:28 Omar Patel: Yes. Stream partial outputs and use prefix caching. If your prefix is common across requests, cache the KV for that prefix and reuse. That reduces per-request token decode.
08:42 Leah Kim: Is cross-pod KV sharing safe for PII? We need to ensure KV stores are encrypted and access-controlled.
08:49 Omar Patel: Absolutely — use in-transit TLS + at-rest KMS encryption, RBAC for memcached/redis endpoints, and minimal network ACLs. We'll document encryption options for the L2 cache.
09:04 Priya Verma: Let's capture sharp next steps and a proposed schedule.
09:10 Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to send runbook + arch diagrams + quantization guidance. Omar to prepare perf harness and test plan. Northleaf to share route tables, NAT/logs, and resolver configs. We'll schedule the lab week of 6/19 for a 1-day deep run.
09:28 Samir Rao: Sounds good. One more question — any quick hotfix we can do without infra changes?
09:34 Omar Patel: Yes — bump conntrack timeouts, enable TLS session tickets, increase TCP keepalive, and temporarily add an L2 memcached on a local subnet. Those changes are low-risk and can be reversed.
09:48 Evan Rivera: We'll try the TLS and conntrack tweaks this week and report back.
09:52 Maya Chen: Perfect. Thanks everyone — we'll share notes and link repository after this call.
09:56 (end)
